futurists-ai-researchers-and-tech-builde.headline: Futurists, AI Researchers & Tech Builders - Visions Trade-Offs Ethics
futurists-ai-researchers-and-tech-builde.author: Bhavisha Patel
futurists-ai-researchers-and-tech-builde.core: Posted in last 7 days Futurists, AI Researchers & Tech Builders - Visions Trade-Offs Ethics A recurring theme I’ve noticed is that it’s really difficult to imagine the future. It’s easy to dismiss an idea … who would want that? Or decide it’s too complicated; it's something I can think about later. I’ve experienced this throughout my tech career. When I was a student studying computer science, over two decades ago, there were actually people telling me what was coming. I just didn’t have the foresight to understand what it would mean. A friend told me his supervisor had said that, in the future, every phone would have the internet. Another friend, who was really into mobile phones, told me that phones would eventually become like mini computers, with something called “apps” that would let you do things on your phone. One of my friends used machine learning for a university project. Her program had to run all night. My dissertation was about finding the shortest route between two points. Google Maps existed, but I remember it being much more like a digital map. I remember thinking that one day it would probably be able to work out the shortest route for you. Looking back, these things seem obvious. They weren’t obvious to me then. And I think that’s the interesting thing about the future. Even when we’re told what’s coming, it can be incredibly difficult to imagine how profoundly it might change the world around us. And we’re doing it again. Except this time, the stakes feel much higher. I’ve been speaking to people about the future and asking what kind of world they want to live in. They talk about climate change. Wealth inequality. Housing. Job opportunity. Peace. So the question I keep coming back to is: What does a better future for everyone actually look like? I want to speak to the people who are shaping what comes next — the people building, researching and thinking about the future. What are they trying to achieve? What kind of trade-offs are they making, and what kind of ethical questions are they asking themselves? I want to have deep conversations about what’s coming, what it could mean for us, and how we might stir ourselves towards building something better.

machine-identity-vendors-ai-agent-delega.headline: Machine Identity Vendors - AI Agent Delegation Solutions
machine-identity-vendors-ai-agent-delega.author: Darshangiri Goswami
machine-identity-vendors-ai-agent-delega.core: Posted in last 7 days Machine Identity Vendors - AI Agent Delegation Solutions Two days at Cybersec Netherlands in Utrecht, and one question followed me across the entire floor. Who owns the identity that is not a person? Some context: Cybersec Netherlands is the largest B2B security event in the Benelux, two days at Jaarbeurs Utrecht, roughly 10,000 visitors. The floor covered almost every domain in the field: OT and ICS security, threat intelligence, data protection, supply chain and resilience, compliance automation, digital sovereignty, and IAM. The theme that kept coming back was AI sitting on both sides of the table. Defenders using it for detection and triage, attackers using it to move faster than a SOC can respond. Mandy Andress of Elastic made the point in her keynote that compliance-driven security models are hitting their limit. That is exactly where non-human identity comes in. Service accounts, API keys, workload identities and now AI agents already outnumber human users in most enterprises. The market is clearly moving on it. Three examples from the floor: Elimity is mapping who can access what across both human and non-human identities, AI agents included, and turning that into access reviews an auditor will accept. Evertrust is doing certificate lifecycle management and sovereign PKI, which is machine identity at its most literal, while preparing customers for shorter TLS lifespans and post-quantum crypto. Kiteworks came at it from the data side. Their own research says most organisations already run AI agents in production, and a majority cannot enforce limits on what those agents do with regulated data, or stop one that misbehaves. Real progress. But look at what all three are solving: visibility, lifecycle, containment. The harder question sits one step further out. An AI agent receives delegated authority from a human and then acts on it. Who approved that scope? Who revokes it when the human leaves? Which control, in which framework, actually covers it? My MSc thesis is a gap analysis of that question across ISO/IEC 27001:2022, NIST CSF 2.0, SOC 2, the DORA RTS and NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5. Three findings I keep coming back to: Not one of the five mandates a rotation cadence for machine secrets. All five are silent on agentic delegated authority. IA-9 in SP 800-53 is the only NHI-native control in any of them, and it is classified P0 and assigned to no baseline. So the tooling runs ahead while the frameworks still work from a registration-era model, where an identity is created once by a human and reviewed quarterly. Machine-speed sprawl walks straight past that. That gap is what I work on. Thesis goes in this month, and I am speaking on NHI governance at Identity Fabric Impact Day 2026. KuppingerCole Analysts If you were at Cybersec and saw a vendor with a real answer for agent delegation, I want to hear about it. Cybersec Netherlands #CybersecNetherlands #NonHumanIdentity #IAM #AISecurity #GRC #Cybersecurity KuppingerCole Ana

At one point, I convinced it to write a whole new version of an article (it was bad), and it never pushed back on my ideas — instead, it often offered to rewrite, revise, reframe, and even draft on my behalf.
